problem: Social robot navigation has no agreed definition and no common evaluation methodology. Prior work uses close to a hundred different metrics, ad-hoc scenarios, incompatible simulators and APIs, and heterogeneous datasets, so results from different groups, robots and simulators cannot be fairly compared.
motivation: Clear, repeatable and accessible benchmarks sped up progress in computer vision, NLP and traditional robot navigation. Social navigation is harder to benchmark because it involves dynamic human agents and their subjective perception of the robot's behavior. Discussions at the 2022 Social Navigation Symposium showed a wide spread of definitions and evaluation setups, which prompted a community consensus effort on definitions, a taxonomy and evaluation guidelines.
key_idea: The paper defines a socially navigating robot as one that reaches its goals while modifying its behavior so that other agents' experience is not degraded or is even enhanced. It unpacks this into eight principles (safety, comfort, legibility, politeness, social competency, agent understanding, proactivity, contextual appropriateness), from which it derives concrete guidelines for metrics, scenarios, benchmarks, datasets and simulators, plus a unified metrics API across simulators, robots and datasets.
insight: Framed as optimization, the first seven principles act as extra objectives on top of reaching the goal, and the eighth (context: cultural, diversity, geometric/operational environment, task, interpersonal) reweights them. The implication is that no single fixed metric or protocol fits all social navigation work, so the intended context must be specified explicitly. Evaluation is best seen as a lifecycle: field studies, robot deployments and staged interactions supply data; issue discovery turns that into validated scenarios; scenarios feed benchmarks and challenges. Benchmarks should combine real-world human evaluation (validated questionnaires) with simulation ablations. There are no experiments or ablations. The simulator analysis does expose a key trade-off: replayed real trajectories are realistic but non-reactive, while reactive models (SFM/ORCA) react but are imperfect. It also finds that fragmented simulator APIs are a main obstacle to comparable metrics, which motivates computing metrics along a single code path.
method: Definition and principles: defines social robot navigation and eight principles, P1 safety through P8 contextual appropriateness, with context split into cultural, diversity, environmental (geometric/operational), task and interpersonal.

Research methodology and lifecycle: catalogs the scientific questions (method comparison, ablations, generalization, human ratings, behavior analysis, issue discovery) and study types (field studies, robot deployments, lab experiments, scenarios, staged interactions); arranges them into a lifecycle from data collection and issue discovery to scenarios, benchmarks and challenges; adds real-world guidelines R1-R3.

Taxonomy of factors: a shared vocabulary (context, physical environment, human user type, human behavior, robot task/role, scenarios, coverage, hardware, sensors, actuators, communication, data/metrics collected, behavior authoring), plus factors specific to datasets and to simulators.

Metrics, scenario and benchmark guidelines: M1-M8 (e.g., report widely used metrics, validate first with algorithmic metrics, use validated surveys), N1-N8 including a 'scenario card' modeled on model cards, and B1-B6 (e.g., include baselines; efficient/repeatable/scalable, with a rule of thumb of at least 30 real-robot trials; ground human evaluations in human data).

Dataset and simulator review: compares datasets (JRDB, THOR, SCAND, MuSoHu, LCAS, ETH/UCY, TrajNet++, EIFPD, SDD, EFL, WILDTRACK, CrowdBot, DynaBARN, SocNav1/2, SACSoN, SG-LSTM) and simulators (CrowdBot, CrowdNav, DynaBARN, gym-collision-avoidance, HuNavSim, iGibson, InHuS, IMHuS, MengeROS, PedSimROS, SEAN 2.0, SocialGym 2.0, SocNavBench) along the taxonomy (Tables V/VI); gives guidelines D1-D8 and S1-S9.

Unified Social Navigation metrics API: a JSON-schema input specification (per-timestep poses of pedestrians/agents, robot observations/actions/trajectories, static and dynamic obstacle geometry), reference metric libraries in C++/Python, and a JSON output schema. Bridge code for ROS messages and OpenAI Gym info structures (GymCollisionAvoidance first; SEAN 2.0, SocialGym, DynaBARN in progress) lets simulators, robots and datasets compute metrics on a single code path (github.com/SocialNav/SocialNavAPI).

setting.backbone: none (position / guidelines / survey paper; no navigation model proposed)
setting.simulator: none used for experiments; reviews 13 social-nav simulators (e.g., SEAN 2.0, iGibson, SocNavBench, CrowdNav); proposed API targets ROS and OpenAI Gym (GymCollisionAvoidance reference)

numbers_note: No experimental results: this is a community position / guidelines / survey paper. Its tables (metrics Table I, scenario/benchmark tables, datasets Table V, simulators Table VI) are qualitative characterizations, and the metrics and benchmark sections were partly omitted from the provided text.
results: There are no quantitative results. The contributions are: (a) a definition of social robot navigation with eight principles; (b) a taxonomy and a set of labeled guidelines covering real-world studies, metrics, scenarios (including a scenario card), benchmarks, datasets and simulators; (c) a qualitative comparison of 16 datasets and 13 simulators; (d) a design and in-progress open-source implementation of a unified metrics API across Gym/ROS simulators, robots and datasets.
limitations: No empirical validation: the guidelines and the API are not tested by running baselines across simulators to show improved comparability.
The unified metrics API was still under development at publication; bridges existed or were planned only for a few systems (ROS, GymCollisionAvoidance; SEAN 2.0, SocialGym, DynaBARN in progress).

The work is consensus-driven, and several issues remain unresolved, including a crisp definition of context and whether learned metrics can replace human evaluations. It covers social navigation among humans, not language- or goal-conditioned embodied navigation benchmarks.
builds_on: Kruse et al. 2013 human-aware navigation survey (comfort, naturalness, sociability principles)
Gao & Huang 2021 evaluation of socially-aware navigation
Mavrogiannis et al. core challenges of social robot navigation
